x-m-h3-01.goal: Know definite integral value and area fit differ; find first error in solution, then choose way to fix am.

x-m-h3-01.s.s1.line.0: Let f(x)=x²−4x+3, and let S be area between curve and x-axis over [0, 3].
x-m-h3-01.s.s1.line.1: Set S=∫₀³ f(x) dx. (definite integral from 0 to 3)
x-m-h3-01.s.s1.line.4: So S=0. Though region between curve and x-axis clearly dey, area come out 0.
x-m-h3-01.s.s1.explain: Calculations lines 3 and 4 correct. Setup line 2 wrong. Definite integral count above-axis part as + and below as −, so 4/3 over [0,1] cancel −4/3 over [1,3] to make 0. Area no use signs, so line 5 conclusion also wrong because setup wrong.

x-m-h3-01.s.s2.r.a: Upper and lower parts cancel to 0. Taking absolute value after cancellation no bring both areas back.
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.o.b: Skip interval where curve below axis; integrate only where above
x-m-h3-01.s.s2.r.b: Below-axis part still enclosed region. Only its sign negative; area positive.

x-m-h3-01.s.s2.r.d: Curve no be straight line, so average endpoint values no represent whole curve.

x-m-h3-02.s.s1.explain: Position change add movement with direction signs, so going and coming cancel. Distance add everything without direction. So position change fit be 0 while distance above 0.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.prompt: For v(t)=t−c, make 2 (c,b) pairs with different c where position change from 0 to b na 0 and distance at least 9.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.hint.0: For position change 0, how areas above and below v(t) graph and t-axis relate?
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.hint.1: Split before and after t=c, calculate both areas. Distance na sum of areas.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.ok.c1: c positive and b greater than c.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.fail.c1: c must positive and b greater than c.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.ok.c2: Position change from 0 to b na 0.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.explain: If position change 0, b=2c, and distance then c². So if c≥3 distance at least 9. Example c=3,b=6: 4.5 left and 4.5 right, total distance 9.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.prompt: Choose one example and use numbers to explain why distance no be 0 even though position change na 0.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write leftward amount and rightward amount as numbers separately.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write what happen to both amounts in position change.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Your explanation show going and return cancel for position change but add for distance?
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Your calculation using chosen c,b correct?
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.model.0: If c=3,b=6, from 0 to 3 e move 4.5 left; from 3 to 6 e move 4.5 right and return. Position change 0, distance 4.5+4.5=9.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.because.model.1: If c=4,b=8, first half 8 left and second half 8 right; dem cancel so position change 0, distance=8+8=16.
x-m-h3-02.s.s2.fail.c2: Position change from 0 to b (= b²/2 − c·b) no be 0.

x-m-h3-03.title: If terms approach 0, sum stop too?
x-m-h3-03.goal: As data collect, reconsider guess ‘terms approach 0, so sum converge’, then choose explanation why guess fit wrong.
x-m-h3-03.material: Sequence aₙ=1/n approach 0 as n grow. Student say, ‘Since terms approach 0, sum 1+1/2+1/3+1/4+… go approach one number too.’ Call sum through n-th term Sₙ (partial sum). Data show step by step.
x-m-h3-03.thinking.0: Guess from partial-sum data and revise with new data
x-m-h3-03.thinking.2: Separate necessary and sufficient for convergence
x-m-h3-03.prereq.0: Know sequence limit and series partial sums
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.prompt: Data go show bit by bit. Each time choose most reasonable judgment.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, compare new data with earlier guess and see where dem differ.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.info: S₁=1, S₂=1.5, S₃≈1.83, S₄≈2.08, S₈≈2.72, S₁₆≈3.38. New terms get smaller.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: From data so far, what judgment reasonable?
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.after: All terms positive, so Sₙ keep increasing. Increasing sequence either approach a number or grow forever; data alone no show which.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Since terms approach 0, Sₙ soon stop at one value
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: Terms getting smaller and sum stopping different things. Tiny amounts fit pile up if you keep adding forever.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Sₙ grow, but need more data to know if e go stop
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You talk only what data support and think what more needed.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.o.c: S₁₆ about 3.38, so sum go stop around 3.38
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You treat sum through 16 terms as final. Terms continue to add forever.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: Sₙ keep increasing, so sure say sum grow forever
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Increasing no mean growing forever. 1/2+1/4+1/8+… increase too but approach 1.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.info: Check sum increase whenever number of terms double: S₂−S₁=0.5, S₄−S₂≈0.58, S₈−S₄≈0.63, S₁₆−S₈≈0.66.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: How this data change your judgment?
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.after: If increase at least 0.5 each time term count double, maybe e keep adding and grow forever. But only through 16 terms, so no proof yet.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Increase settles around 0.66, so e only grow by dat and stop soon
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: If e increase about 0.6 each time, amount keep piling. Main thing na whether increase amount approach 0.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.o.b: My first guess: terms approach 0, so sum stop
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You no update first judgment using new data. New clue: increase amount no reduce.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Increase amount no fall below 0.5, so sum probably no stop
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You revise first guess with new data. Remember this still no be proof.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.after: For 1 + 1/2 + (1/3 + 1/4) + (1/5 + … + 1/8) + …, each group add more than 1/2, without end, so partial sum dey grow without end. Even if terms dey close to 0, sum no necessarily converge.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Still no fit tell. I need calculate larger n before I decide
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Problem still be say calculation no dey end. Comparing groups let you make statement without endless calculation.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Each group bigger than 1/2 and dem continue forever, so sum dey grow forever
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You judge by the fact say at least 1/2 keep piling up for every group, without end.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Each group about 1/2, so sum too go close to about 1/2
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: No be one group only; dem keep going. Wetin happen if you keep adding at least 1/2 forever?
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Terms inside groups dey smaller, so e go eventually close to some number
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: Even if terms dey smaller, sum of one group no go smaller than 1/2.
x-m-h3-03.s.s1.reflect: If you first think “terms dey close to 0, so sum too go stop,” which information make you change your mind? Terms approaching 0 na necessary or sufficient condition for sum to stop?
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.prompt: Based on results above, choose correct statement about relationship between terms aₙ and series Σaₙ.
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.hint.0: Remember relationship between partial sum Sₙ and term aₙ (aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁).
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.hint.1: Test whether example 1/n from above fit each statement.
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.o.a: If Σaₙ converge, then aₙ dey close to 0
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.r.a: This judgment look at wetin limit of converging series mean for terms.
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.o.b: If aₙ dey close to 0, then Σaₙ always converge
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.r.b: Example 1/n na counterexample. Terms getting smaller alone no guarantee say sum go stop.
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.o.c: If Σaₙ diverge, then aₙ no dey close to 0
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.r.c: 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + … diverge, but terms dey close to 0.
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.o.d: Even if aₙ no dey close to 0, Σaₙ fit converge
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.r.d: If terms no dey close to 0, increases in partial sum keep remaining, so e no fit converge.
x-m-h3-03.s.s2.explain: If Σaₙ converge, increase in partial sum, aₙ = Sₙ − Sₙ₋₁, dey close to 0. But the reverse no always work. 1/n na counterexample.

x-m-h3-05.title: Two Games at Festival Booth: Which One to Play?
x-m-h3-05.goal: Check whether expected value alone enough when comparing two games, explain the standard for choosing by making new game yourself wey satisfy conditions.
x-m-h3-05.material: Two games dey at festival booth. Game A: flip coin; if head prize na 100 won, if tail 0 won. Game B: draw one ball from box; if e be winner (probability 1/10), prize na 500 won, otherwise 0 won. Both games no get entry fee, and call prize random variable X.
x-m-h3-05.thinking.0: Judge whether expected value alone enough
x-m-h3-05.thinking.1: Design one game yourself (probability and prize) wey fit condition
x-m-h3-05.thinking.2: Give evidence for reason behind your choice
x-m-h3-05.prereq.0: Learn by putting probability mass function of discrete random variable in table
x-m-h3-05.prereq.1: Understand wetin mean of random variable represent
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose correct explanation comparing the two games.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.hint.0: Calculate expected value for each game directly as (prize × probability), then compare.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write possible prizes for each game.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.o.a: A get higher expected value. Because chance of winning higher
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.r.a: You look only at probability, no consider prize size too.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.o.b: B get higher expected value. Because prize 5 times bigger
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.r.b: You look only at prize, no consider chance of winning too.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.o.c: Expected values same, but how spread out prizes dey different
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.r.c: You point out say even when expected values same, distribution shape fit different.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.o.d: Expected values same, so results same whichever game you play
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.r.d: Expected value na only “average over many plays,” e no tell one result or how spread out dem be.
x-m-h3-05.s.s1.explain: E(A) = 100 × 1/2 = 50 and E(B) = 500 × 1/10 = 50, so dem equal. But A prize na 0 won or 100 won, and B na 0 won or 500 won, so B spread out much more.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 new games with different winning probabilities, expected value 50 won, and prize at least 400 won. (If you win, prize na m won; if no, 0 won.)
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.hint.0: Using condition say expected value na 50, write relationship between p and m as equation.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.hint.1: Choose m first, then adjust p.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.fail.c1: Probability must bigger than 0 and smaller than 1.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.fail.c2: Expected value (p × m) no be 50 won.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.explain: p × m = 50, so if m=400 then p=0.125; if m=1000 then p=0.05. Bigger prize, smaller chance of winning.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Compare one game you make with Game A, and write which one you rather play and why, pointing to expected value. No one correct answer only.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Write at beginning say expected values equal.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write one standard of your own, like “I be the kind of person wey ...”
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: You first agree say expected values equal, then state your own standard too?
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Your choice connect to standard like “whether you like or dislike taking risks”?
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.model.0: Both expected values na 50 won, so average same. I want receive something steadily and often, so I go play A, wey get higher chance of winning. Game with low probability get big variance, so I fit no get anything once.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.model.1: Even though expected values same, I like take risk and aim for big prize, so I go choose game with 500 won prize. Even if winning chance low, big prize fit come at once.
x-m-h3-05.s.s2.because.model.2: Even though expected value same, 50 won, I prefer collect small amount safely, so I rather play Game A. For game with low probability, you fit no win even once.

x-m-h3-10.title: Two perpendicular lines parallel?
x-m-h3-10.goal: Make coordinate counterexample yourself to check claim true on plane may fail in space.
x-m-h3-10.material: On plane, two lines perpendicular to one line parallel. Check coordinates whether true in space. In space, line n direction vector n=(1, 2, 2) (components one, two, two). Direction vectors l,m na u=(u1,u2,u3) and v=(v1,v2,v3); both perpendicular to n.
x-m-h3-10.thinking.0: Reason about difference between plane and space
x-m-h3-10.thinking.1: Make vector pairs satisfying conditions (perpendicular, not parallel)
x-m-h3-10.prereq.0: Practice writing vectors with space coordinates
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.prompt: Choose correct statement about ‘two lines perpendicular to one line are parallel.’
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.hint.0: Draw how many directions perpendicular to one line on plane.
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.hint.1: Imagine how many directions perpendicular to line in space (like directions around upright pencil).
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.o.a: Always true on plane and in space
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.r.a: You carry plane experience straight to space. In space, there can be more than one perpendicular direction.
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.o.b: True in space, with plane counterexample
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.r.b: Think how many perpendicular directions one line get on plane.
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.o.c: True on plane, counterexample in space
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.r.c: You separate plane and space difference.
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.o.d: Counterexamples dey both on plane and in space
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.r.d: Check whether plane get only one direction perpendicular to a line.
x-m-h3-10.s.s1.explain: On plane, only one perpendicular direction, so both lines parallel. In space, many perpendicular directions lie in one plane, so lines no always parallel.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.prompt: Choose integer components for u and v, both perpendicular to n=(1, 2, 2) and not parallel to each other, then make 2 different pairs. (Pair with u/v order switched count as same.)
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.hint.0: Write condition for u perpendicular to n as equation in components. Find one integer vector wey meet am.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.hint.1: Find v wey no be constant multiple of u you find. E easier if you set one component to 0.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.ok.c3: u and v no parallel (and neither one na zero vector).
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.fail.c3: u and v parallel, or one of dem na zero vector.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.explain: u=(2, −1, 0) and v=(0, 1, −1) both perpendicular to n, and neither vector na constant multiple of other. Plenty directions perpendicular to n dey in one plane, so as many non-parallel pairs as you like.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.because.prompt: Looking at pair you make, explain in one or 2 sentences why wetin be parallel in a plane no hold for space.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.because.hint.0: Compare how many perpendicular directions dey in plane and in space.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.because.hint.1: Put components of u and v you choose inside your sentences.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: My explanation show say “plenty perpendicular directions dey, no be only one”?
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: You explain by including components of u and v you make?
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.because.model.0: Vectors perpendicular to n no be only one direction like u=(2, −1, 0); dem plenty, so v=(0, 1, −1) also perpendicular but no parallel to u. Na because perpendicular directions spread across plane.
x-m-h3-10.s.s2.because.model.1: (2, −1, 0) and (2, 0, −1) both perpendicular to n=(1, 2, 2), but dem be different directions. For plane, only one perpendicular direction dey; for space, many directions perpendicular to n, so parallel rule no hold.
